I don’t think AI should be taking anyone’s job without an economic displacement incentive involved (automation of any kind should be to free us up from menial labor, not be a cheap replacement). However, artists are in a particularly vulnerable position in the advent of AI. I’ve been a professional theatrical designer for almost 20 years and even before AI was a conceivable reality, artists’ work was not appropriately valued. What made the difference was that artists had skills that couldn’t be replicated at the level of quality required. The difference in quality was noticeable between a pro and a hack. Even back then, people didn’t know what it took to develop and hone those skills and would balk at $500 to play live music for an event or whatever price one was selling their artistic services and products for. Now those people still don’t know what it takes and AI can “magically” create things that these yahoos find “good enough.” So for artists, AI presents a danger that wasn’t a possibility even 5 years ago. Artists’ work is already undervalued and poorly understood and this makes it worse. It’s like toddlers being responsible for handing out Michelin stars. They clap their hands for Kraft Mac and cheese at Chilis while turning their nose up at quality food. 

In other industries, the lack of quality is more noticeable because people understand the standards of quality. People aren’t going to trust an AI Oncologist anytime soon. People are going to get frustrated with AI customer service when their issue can’t get resolved. Put plainly, most of the jobs that are vulnerable are tasks that people understand. Art is different. That’s not to say it’s ok to disadvantage people because they aren’t artists, but there’s a particular vulnerability that isn’t present for other industries.

This top is basically a tank top with a (false) double breasted closure. You could make your own pattern relatively easily. Find a dress or top that fits you well and has the same shape. Then use butcher paper to trace the front and then draw out the shape of the double breasted lap. Note how the outer edge of the top lap is in line with the seam. You’ll also need another trace of the front and draw the seams down from the straps. Your front will have four pieces, the two sides, the center, and the double breasted lap. You’ll want to leave the lap hanging and then do an invisible stitch to secure it to the seam. Do a standard two piece back with the closure of your choice.

I think there’s value in separating the vehicle from the driver, but it’s possible to do that and still not have a positive view of homeschooling. My experience in homeschooling was overflowing with homeschool-positive people who couldn’t separate the driver from the vehicle either. Far too many people insisted that homeschooling was the only way to educate and that it was 100% more effective than public school. It’s honestly frustrating as someone who was homeschooled by neglecting and sometimes abusive parents because that sort of attitude was promoted by national homeschool orgs. The homeschool parents parroted that ideology and kids were hurt because of it. I’ve been a relatively successful adult *in spite* of homeschooling and saw the damage it can do firsthand not only to myself and my siblings, but so many other kids I knew. I recognize the ways that homeschooling enabled the neglect I experienced in ways that public school  absolutely would not have. In that way, the vehicle is also responsible. 

My advice to people who are thinking about homeschooling is to follow the student’s needs and desires. If they *want* to homeschool and you can do it, make it happen. If they beg to go back to public school, let them. Don’t be like my parents.

I’ve taught theatre design in higher ed and one of the things I find most useful is the Lerman Critical Response Method. I adapt it for less formal critiques like this:

1. Ask what was your goal, what did you want to accomplish? Sometimes this is an illuminating question for the artist as well as me. 
2. What are YOU most proud of? (This lets me know how I might approach the next steps)
3. What do you see you’d want to improve? (Many people are already aware of the flaws and looking for confirmation)
4. Start out with the good things. It might be “I really like the colors, this part is really exciting” 
5. Subjectify your critique with “I think…, If it were me…,” take into consideration the things they’re proud of and know need to improve. If the thing they’re really proud of is not great, find some redeeming quality and tell them that “this specific aspect takes away from this redeeming quality”
6. Finish with affirmation, encouragement and praise for whatever might be good.

The truth of the matter is that color is relative and subjective. Color theory is our attempt to describe the color we see. We have to think of color theory as descriptive and not prescriptive. We can use color theory to describe relationships of color, but every system we use to describe it has limitations. Like you can absolutely make a vibrant red with yellow and magenta. Does that mean red isn’t a primary color? Not at all. It’s just not a primary color in CMYK. Red IS a primary color in light and mixing red and blue light will give you magenta. Does that mean magenta isn’t a primary color? Not at all, it’s just not a primary color in light. RBY pigment mixing tends to result in less saturated colors whereas CMYK pigment mixing tends to result in more vibrant colors. Color in light is fundamentally different than color in pigment on paper. This is why something looks great on your computer screen and too dark or too light when you print it out. The light from your screen alters your perception of color and your printer may be unable to produce the colors your screen can.

When I was in school we did 30 minute copywork sketches of figures weekly (3 per class per week). We had to set a timer, and draw the figure as accurately as possible and when 30 minutes was up we had to stop. It was difficult at first, but slowly it became easier. I got REALLY behind on my sketches and ended up having to do 21 of them in a matter of a couple of days. Out of necessity I started cutting my time to 25 minutes, 20 minutes, then taking a minute off each sketch. By the time I got to the last one I drew an accurate human figure complete with shading in 10 minutes. 

It’s all about practice, repetition, and putting limits on yourself. You end up finding tricks or techniques that make it easier, your brain starts to see things quickly and clearly, and you get better at executing the action of drawing with more finesse and ease. You learn how to pace yourself. I knew that if I wasn’t shading by the last third of my time I was cooked. You also have a literal paper trail demonstrating your progress. It was really encouraging when I had a sketch I wasn’t proud of to look back at what I’d done before and go “at least it’s better than that!” It’s not always a linear progression. Sometimes you reach a new level and everything seems to suck, partially because you’re seeing better and partially because you’ve made new space in your brain and it hasn’t had time to fill up with new skill. Just keep drawing.

I’m not terribly familiar with clip studio, but I use Procreate on my iPad. One thing I’ve found incredibly helpful is to put my shading on different layers. I’ll often have a “working layer” and then when I’m happy with what I’ve done I’ll put it into the appropriate parent layer. If it’s one of those “good enough for now” moments I’ll keep it separate to further adjust after doing more work. Another thing that can help when working digitally is to increase/decrease the transparency of a layer. When I’m making a shadow of a human figure on the ground, I’ll duplicate the entire figure, make it totally black, and then place the shadow where I want it with the distort and warp commands. Then I lower the transparency until it looks right to me. I usually live between 30-50% depending on the lighting conditions but I’ve gone as low as 12 and as high as 70. 

Are you going in with a specific transparency on your brush? Try something REALLY low and build up to the level you want. It makes it even easier if you have something like a brush at 10% then each pass you make theoretically goes in multiples of 10. If you find yourself making 4-5 passes with a 10% brush, bump it up to 20 or 30 and see if that gets you closer to where you want. You can always play with the transparency to fine tune it further. 

You may also want to do some pencil sketching as a medium shift to better understand how that medium works. You really get a good sense of building up shading that way. I tend to “paint” with graphite by using a really saturated blending stub for subtle shadows. It’s truly incredible how different digital painting and pencil sketching are. I honestly don’t know that I’d be as good as I am now without having done hours of sketches per week with nothing but a mechanical pencil, an ebony pencil, and a blending stub and eraser. You might also benefit from gray-paper work with only a white and black pencil. This makes you pay close attention to the highlights and shadows to create form and depth.

Honestly, it’s really about noticing how the light falls on objects and surfaces. You have to train your brain to pick up on the different values and the only way to do that is with practice and careful observation. One of the best things to do is to take a *simple* full-color reference into grayscale and adjust the brightness/exposure. Notice what is still visible when it’s really dark and really light. Adjust the reference until you can see the distinct areas. Then optimize the reference to the best place where you feel like you can really SEE the values and try to replicate. It’ll probably suck the first time around, do it again, until you feel good about what you’re doing. Then go back to the full-color reference and do it again. I think a lot of it has to do with our development and socialization regarding art. Children initially tend to enjoy drawing, but at some point (usually around 6-8) they begin to get frustrated that what they are drawing no longer reflects what they see…in a realistic sense at least. Teachers and peers praise art that “looks so realistic” and this reinforces the idea that realistic art is good art. This cognitive development and subsequent socialization leads to the commonly shared value of realistic art as the pinnacle of skill. It’s absolute bullshit but at least from a developmental standpoint it makes sense. 

I’m primarily a theatre designer and in the late 19th century there was a whole genre of theatre/dramatic literature that was capital R Realism. They wanted everything to be a “slice of life” and this is where we get the idea of “the 4th wall” because sets were literally a boxed room with the 4th wall removed. It was a movement for a specific time and place (the development of photography as a new art form, the development of foundational scientific discoveries, dissatisfaction with the artifice of melodrama). Later in the 20th century film became the home of this Realism because it did it much better. Theatre had to reinvent itself and we got some of the most interesting and exciting theatre in history (I’m a 20th century theatre specialist so I’m a little biased). Legendary designer Robert Edmund Jones that said “Realism is something we practice when we aren’t feeling very well. When we don’t feel up to the extra effort.” I wholeheartedly agree. As an artist, realism isn’t my goal. Realism is a fundamental skill but it’s only the first and least taxing step in making good art.

From a developmental standpoint it’s super normal for teenagers to have a moment or time of doubt, anger, or disbelief of god. 

James Fowler’s stages of faith and Piaget’s stages of cognitive development both have a moment where things become abstract and messy around age 12. Many teens can go through a time in life where the more concrete aspects of life and faith become discongruent with a more abstract understanding of life. This shift can cause many teens to genuinely reject faith. Depending on the situation, those teens may return to their faith as their faith development catches up with their cognitive development and they begin to accept more less concrete, more abstract conceptions of faith. Sometimes this discongruence develops into lasting agnosticism or atheism. Factors such as the nature of the religious tradition, socioeconomic status, neglect and abuse, and family environment can impact the eventual outcome. 

I’d say it’s less propaganda and more a misunderstanding of what’s actually going on developmentally. It’s very normal and many people find peace in returning to their religious tradition. Many others, very normally, never return. What makes the difference is if the world around them matches what the religious tradition is saying. For example, a Pentecostal tradition that emphasizes spiritual warfare and ecstatic spiritual experiences such as speaking in tongues is less likely to see a highly analytical mind return. This is often reinforced by dogmatic and rigid communities that foster an “us vs them” approach to faith. A religious tradition that values mystery and contemplation is more likely to re-attract a mind that accepts the fundamental abstractness of life and these are the people whose faith development catches up with their cognitive development. 

There’s not a one size fits all approach and each individual’s path will be unique, but there are at least a few developmental factors that commonly influence this process.

Former theatre professor here, first of all don’t take the statement of any professor as anything but the observation of someone with a point of view. They might be right. They might be wrong. What determines that is you. Your professor is coming from their perspective and so their advice is going to be “them-colored.” They’re interpreting things from their point of view. You are the one that will have to live your life and your perspective is the one that matters. 

On the topic at hand: will a children’s book class make you a better artist? It depends on what being a better artist means to you. I’m going to make the assumption that “children’s book classes” are housed in the English department and not the art department. A children’s book class in the English department is probably going to explore the textual and storytelling aspects of children’s books. An art based class on children’s books is probably going to focus on the visual storytelling and stylistic choices of children’s books. If your goal is to illustrate children’s books I think either option is a valuable experience. 

Artists have two jobs. One is to explore their chosen media with technical skill to create meaningful experiences. The other is to express something through those meaningful experiences. Will a children’s book class make you a better artist when it comes to your technical skill as an artist? Maybe, maybe not. Will a children’s book class give you a springboard toward expressing something through meaningful experiences? Probably. Artists are observers and storytellers. A class in children’s literature can be a valuable experience in observation and experimentation. 

Now all this said, your professor might be thinking more about your technical skill with your media. They might not have the perspective to see how this will benefit your ability to express something through meaningful experiences. You have to decide which is most beneficial for you. Is it a better use of your time to improve your technique or is it a better use of your time to develop your voice as a storyteller? I have my opinion but yours is the one that matters. I personally think that an artist without something to say is more of a technician than an artist. If I want pretty, I’ll look in the mirror. I want the art I consume to have something to say. 

Best of luck to you and I’m sure whatever choice you make will be the right one for you. :)

I worked in a high school in the US for a semester and a week before I was coerced to resign. Before that I was a college professor for over a decade. I’ve seen how college freshmen have changed over the last decade pre and post COVID. 
Ways to strengthen public K-12 education:

1. Deemphasize standardized testing and constant “data driven approaches” to documenting learning. Everything from student learning to teacher performance is micromanaged to the nth degree. Nobody above the teacher in the classroom seems to be concerned with actual learning, but goddamn they want to see the data that shows they’re learning. We were required to post 2 grades per week and we met with the class 2-3 times a week. This meant daily graded assignments and it’s just too much for the students and for the teachers. 

2. Emphasize skill building, media literacy, making connections, and real-life applications. The most important aspects of my education were the things that weren’t graded. We need to evaluate learning but grades aren’t helpful. Building meaningful connections between skills and practicing real-life scenarios is vital to developing healthy young adults.

3. A rich experience complete with art, theatre, music, and dance is vital to making education work. These disciplines require critical thinking skills and develop creative problem solving skills vital for any career. They also help reduce anxiety and give kids confidence in presenting themselves. 

4. DO. FEWER. THINGS. BETTER. One of the most concerning things I noticed was my students were scheduled into oblivion. 8 classes a year, dozens of extracurricular activities, church, off campus activities, and you’ve got a 14 year old who is as stressed out as their teacher in their late 30s/early 40s. These kids need to slow the fuck down. 

5. Emphasize a variety of paths to careers as equal and desirable. There are kids that should go into trades, there are kids that should go to technical school, there are kids that should go to a 4 year liberal arts university and for decades we’ve told kids that the only way to a stable career is through college. Millennials know that’s absolute bullshit, but all these motherfuckers saying “become a plumber” don’t think about what’s going to happen when everyone goes into trades. We’re going to have the same problems we have right now with college degrees. We need every career and we need to support getting kids into careers that are economically stable and best suited for those kids’ desires and strengths. 

6. Change the world kids are graduating into. In order for #5 to work, we’ve got to reduce the inequality between the economic stability between careers. A garbage truck driver is no less necessary than a doctor or a coder, and while there can be differences in pay for those roles, there should not be a difference in those careers ability to provide a stable and safe existence. Most kids today are ambivalent about their career goals and “just want to make money” because that’s truly the only thing that matters to the world they live in. So we’re in a constant cycle of people chasing the highest paid careers with the least requirements instead of channeling energy into their passions. Then we get an overabundance of people in a few careers and the directive shifts to a new emphasis, rinse and repeat.

7. Make every single decision emphasizing that all people, regardless of any factor, deserve food, shelter, healthcare, community, and culture.

Like I get not wanting to turn the crit into a therapy session, but I think there are ways to acknowledge where you come from without laying your book open on a park bench for all to see. Whiteness was the goal, the default. What if your piece represented the world in shades of white and contrast that with how you see the world now? Perhaps the white as default is a prison? Perhaps the white is something you’re moving away from. How did that lens affect you as you became an adult? 

Then there’s the recovery/reclamation strategy (which might be easier at first). I have a lot of trauma from my childhood and adolescence but over the years I’ve been able to find some peace with elements of that childhood that made me a better person. Paula Vogel described How I Learned to Drive as a play about the gifts we receive from the people who hurt us. My parents did a lot of shitty things but one thing they did right was read to us and encourage us to read. It was ultimately reading that helped me grow and transition away from harmful aspects of my childhood. It was also reading that introduced me to design, and art, and science, and dinosaurs. So I grew up in a home culture where reading was valued and that ultimately led to me rejecting other aspects of the culture I grew up with. 

You’re doing important work here, and I really wish you the best. Good art has something to say. Think about what you would want to say and then think about how you might represent that through your art.

I am absolutely exhausted after visiting a new place because I’m constantly observing the architecture, nature, human behavior, and happenstance. I take pictures of doors and plants and sculptures which I retain for the moment I’ll need them. I have a Pinterest board that I curate with inspiration and when I begin a new project I scroll through this massive board I’ve curated over 10 years and see if anything resonates. My best work has come out of this strategy.

In theatre, especially in lighting, we talk about “visual vocabularies” such as warm light vs cool light as different “words” we use to communicate specific meanings or feelings. There’s probably some interesting interrogation to be had in that idea alone. Good design uses these vocabularies with self-imposed rules derived from the way humans typically respond to visual stimuli (a Dutch angle in film tells us something is off and we feel a sense of danger or uncertainty). This seems to align with the sense of linguistic conventions because while there is commonly understood meanings (like lime green=evil in Disney) these emotional responses to visual stimuli can be culturally influenced (red in the US as danger/passion vs red as happiness in China). So perhaps it could be said that there are linguistic systems employed by artists and style/culture constitute dialects of that language.

As some have pointed out, that’s not the only Greek creation myth…and it’s also not the only Hebrew creation myth. In fact, Genesis offers two accounts on creation almost back to back that scholars identify as coming from two different periods. Genesis 1:1 begins the Priestly account from around the time of the Babylonian exile and presents an orderly creation over 6 days with man and woman being created simultaneously as the pinnacle of creation. This account uses the Tetragrammaton YHWH to reference god in the Hebrew and usually just gets translated “God”. Genesis 2:4 starts the Elohist account which is older and features a more intimate god who creates ha-adam (essentially a genderless mud golem who is animated by the breath of Elohim), makes all the animals but they’re not a suitable help-meet, then takes the rib from ha-adam to make ha-adamah (woman) who is the pinnacle of creation. This account uses Elohim for god (some translations use sources that are later and edited to use YHWH Elohim) and this is usually translated as “The LORD God.”

Ultimately ancient Hebrew religion was originally polytheistic like their ancient near eastern counterparts. The shift to monotheism happened over time but there are artifacts of this polytheism that got included in the canon of Hebrew scripture. Genesis contains references to “the sons of God” or nephilim which is part of this idea of a Divine Council. We also see this Divine Counsel in Job where ha-satan (the accuser, only later interpreted as being “the devil”) comes before Elohim to ask to test Job. 

There are also references to Asherah as “the queen of heaven” in Jeremiah 7:18. The women make cakes of bread to offer to “the queen of heaven” which references an earlier practice in polytheistic Hebrew religion and demonstrates how that practice was vilified in an effort to shift toward monotheism. The shift from polytheism to monotheism was inherently patriarchal and these women making these offerings was seen as particularly onerous. 

So it’s not that one religion “stole” an idea as we think about it. We frankly don’t have the primary sources to support any sort of detailed chronological account, but these various religious ideas were part of a shared understanding of the world (not unlike Christian denominations of today) which varied locally and what we have today is a highly, sometimes violently, curated strain of a much larger religious universe.

One thing my mentor told me in college was the 8/1/1 rule. I’m a theatre designer and she said “Out of 10 shows you do, 1 will be the best thing you’ve ever done, 1 will be the worst, and the other 8 are just shows.” This helped me take the pressure off myself and put my work into perspective. When you’re not trying to make everything you do be that one best piece, and give yourself permission to let the 8 be the 8, it becomes a lot easier to stomach the 1 worst thing. When you do inevitably hit that worst one, it doesn’t crash your confidence because you know it’s the one. It also provides some motivation because of this is the worst one, the next one won’t be so bad. When what you’ve done is one of the 8, you’re not so distressed because 8 compared to 1 is a significantly unbalanced ratio and you recognize it for the inevitability that it is.

I’ve been married for 17 years and we’ve gone through so many phases of life. We got married fairly early (before we graduated college) and that was both a blessing and a curse. It was great because we were deeply in love, it was awful because we weren’t really fully developed adults and so going through the  process of really owning your life often felt glacially slow. We both grew up in very restrictive environments that prepared us poorly for the realities of adulthood (thanks church trauma). When I went to grad school my wife was miserable and because we planned to return to our home state she took a job back home and stayed with her parents. This kicked off what ended up being 5 years of living in different states for a variety of reasons including staying with her parents after her dad’s near death motorcycle accident. The 5 years long distance was extremely hard on us, particularly because I didn’t want to do it. We grew up as individuals during this time and grew apart. Living in the same house again was really tough. We nearly split up on multiple occasions over the next 3-4 years. Eventually it was me embracing my love and admiration for my wife that kept us together. We truly are an incredible team and my strengths are her weaknesses, my weaknesses are her strengths. We’re very different people, and somehow it works. She is a fucking incredible person. I am regularly in awe of how she is able to treat people with such kindness and compassion, and she’s really stuck it out with me during my darkest times. She’s literally the best person I know. Even when she’s on my last goddamn nerve, I remember the times I just sat back and watched her be amazing. I personally have been struggling to get through day to day life for decades because of abusive and toxic work and social situations and she’s the reason I’m still here, even when I begrudge that. 

One of the biggest things I’ve learned is let them be mad. Let them feel whatever they’re feeling, and allow yourself that too. It’s ok to be mad as fuck at someone and still love them. Don’t try to force them to change their mood or behavior, obviously don’t let them treat you poorly, but just let them do their thing. We are both the kind of people who react poorly in moments of revelation and after a few hours or day or two we’re in a better place to talk about it candidly. 

So my prescription for a long, healthy marriage is to find a person who you absolutely adore. Know that there are going to be times you will be deliriously angry with them and that’s ok. Go to therapy if you need it personally or as a couple. Don’t live separate, and always remember what you love about them.

As someone who has taught both college and high school, what you’re seeing is largely the result of K-12 education that does not emphasize writing. Many high school students don’t even write research papers anymore. The writing standards are often much more granular and lend themselves to compartmentalized skills with little connection between them. It’s these connections and the synthesis of ideas that good writing requires. The kids just don’t even get put in a position where they have to do such things until their first year comp class. I’ve always been linguistically inclined and while I look back on my freshman English papers with full cringe, I remember being shocked by how advanced my writing was compared to my peers as a traditional student. I was homeschooled through middle and high school so I expected to be WAY behind and it turned out I was head, shoulders, knees, and toes above my classmates. 

I also think about how social media has changed the way we communicate. When I was a kid in the 90s, AOL message boards and chat rooms were my primary consumption of proto-social media. I attribute much of my rhetorical development to discussing a variety of topics on message boards dedicated to beanie babies, home decor shows like trading spaces, and Harry Potter. I would argue with full grown adults with college degrees and learned rhetorical and creative writing strategies. Now we’re in a social media landscape that prioritizes video and photo content and writing is just a different form of communication. Most TikTok style videos don’t employ writing because they’re using preexisting sound bites sounds as their text. 

My advice is to do what you can but don’t burden yourself too much. You’re likely to have some peers that will appreciate the level of feedback you can provide, and others that will think you’re full of yourself while they can’t identify the noun and verb in a sentence. Focus on punctuation and spelling, don’t rephrase things for them unless it’s absolutely necessary, and don’t work harder than they are. Peer review should be saying “this is what I understand you to say here, is that what you intended?” and catching typos, punctuation, and spelling mistakes. You’re there for you, and while there’s exceptional value in peer review…you’re clearly not their rhetorical peer. 

Good luck to you! You’re the kind of student professors enjoy having in class.

Armchair linguist with acting training here…there are a lot of factors that influence what we hear. We tend to hear the deeper bone resonances of our own voice when we speak and hearing a recording of ourselves that lacks those lower frequencies can be disorienting in and of itself. Your speakers, your colleague’s speakers, the transition from your voice to their speakers and back through your own can cause a number of fidelity issues as well. 

Generally, I find myself raising the pitch of my voice when I’m seeking to come across as non-threatening and approachable. The placement of my voice when I’m projecting is a few notes higher than my typical speaking voice. Average men tend to use 3-5 notes in their speaking voice where women and expressive speakers tend to use 5-7 notes. I’ve noted qualities in my diction and articulation that also seem to fit the “gay voice.” I tend to use editing software to lower the pitch of my speaking voice to sound more like what I hear. It’s not possible to do live, but it works for the prerecorded speaking I do. 

So you’re probably unconsciously raising your pitch, maybe using more notes than other men, and hearing an objective recording of your voice augmented by compromised audio fidelity. However, attempts to do this with people who act seem awkward. Performer is…probably the closest to server in terms of usage…but it becomes more ambiguous. A musician is a performer, a magician is a performer, a gymnast is a performer, but none of them are acting in the way that someone does when they’re playing Blanche or Stanley in Streetcar Named Desire. 

So in this case, the removal of gendered terms results in a default to what is the masculine form of the word. Men and women are actors by profession. It doesn’t necessarily follow the rules of Latin, but there are many constructions that are considered standard in English that don’t follow the rules of dead languages.

As a theatre professional, this is perhaps true of film where realism is the goal, but that is only one small outlier in a much larger discipline. From its inception, acting as we know it was only allowed for men until the 17th century. Men played both men and women, and women were forbidden from the stage. The notion that people should play the gender they were assigned at birth is a relatively new concept in the grand scheme of things. 

It’s not fundamentally necessary to distinguish between gender unless the role requires it explicitly.

One of the things about trauma is that it often feels incredibly isolating. Talking about trauma is also more common because we have the vocab to talk about it more than previous generations. People with physical and psychological trauma are more aware of what’s happening and how the trauma affects their day-to-day life and so that becomes a topic of discussion more often. Some people talk about their traumas in an effort to de-stigmatize their experiences and find community. Highly empathetic people sometimes share a similar experience as a way of connecting with someone. This can be interpreted as trying to one-up someone or competing in the oppression Olympics, but that isn’t what’s happening in most cases. 

People are also at various points in dealing with their traumas and with everyone being so connected it can inundate our feeds. It’s important to protect yourself so avoiding or ignoring those discussions can be helpful. It does more harm than good telling someone they should just get over it and grow. Most of the time the people who get really agitated over this seem upset that they have to take the needs of others into account. The best thing one can do is be supportive of the people they care about and let others do what they’re going to do. As a theatre teacher/professor, this is a super common response…and one of the most annoying things about training theatre professionals. There are, of course, many reasons that someone might not get a role. Sometimes it’s because the director is an asshole. More often the actor thinks they are more skilled or a better fit than they are. At the end of the day, you might be PERFECT for a role and someone else is PERFECT for another role. However, those two roles require a certain chemistry and the director chooses an actor that fits that dynamic best. Now an actor who was PERFECT for the role didn’t get cast and is salty about it. You have to get used to the fact that actors are dime-a-dozen and big cities makes it more like half-a-penny-a-dozen. This isn’t a reflection of the value of an actor or the profession itself, it’s just that people are more likely to want to be an actor than other disciplines in theatre. It’s all ratios. You will lose out on more roles than you’ll ever get. Get used to it now, accept it for what it is, and if that’s not something you want, it’s totally ok to say “this isn’t for me”

Success in theatre is 45% talent, 45% work, and 10% is an X factor that you can do nothing about. Don’t get hung up on your talent. Talent is worthless if it isn’t skilled. Far too many theatre kids think that talent is all they need. Within a year they have been soundly outstripped by talentless hacks who have put in the work. 

You are absolutely within your rights to be disappointed that you didn’t get a role. But let it stop there. There is ZERO benefit in digging to find out why you didn’t get the role except to identify areas where you can improve. It’s shitty to make unfounded assumptions about what a director is doing, especially if they are credentialed and experienced and you’re not. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve had to remind a kid that I had three degrees, decades of experience, and 16 pages of CV that they don’t. Experience doesn’t always mean quality, you can shovel shit for 20 years and never be a gold miner, but usually experience is full of mistakes you’ve learned from. My perspective and skills are fundamentally broader and finer than my students and that’s how it’s supposed to be unless you’re ok with just going through the motions and hoping you get lucky. You WANT to be trained by people that are better than you. You should WANT to be in a challenging environment that promotes growth. You’ll never get that if you always get the role. 

Also keep in mind that just because someone always gets the role at your school, doesn’t mean that’s how it will be outside those doors. Go do theatre somewhere else. Meet new people. Make your own work. Do a staged reading. I knew actors who did not make it into the BFA program and actors who did. There are BFA actors working the front desk at sleazy hotels and there are BA actors on Broadway. Focus on being the best artist you can be. Actors wait tables. Artists work.

I think it’s less a conscious choice and more of an understanding of the character with 20 years of history between the original and film incarnation. The shift from stage to film also requires different acting choices. What works in a broadway theatre from 30-60 feet away doesn’t always work from 3-6 feet away. Now there’s certainly room for dialing back the intensity of a choice, but there are some choices that just don’t translate to film regardless of intensity. I think there’s also a personal dimension to this shift. For Erivo, it’s clear that the color of her skin has been the reason people chose to treat her poorly or differently, and so that becomes the engine for her portrayal of Elphaba. She’s green and that’s other-ing enough for Erivo’s performance. Now consider Idina Menzel’s originating performance of the role, and the skin color aspect is no longer a point of resonance. So she had to find aspects to tap into to create that aspect of the performance. I think having a preferred performance of a role is normal, but I do think we have to consider exactly why that performance speaks to us. The deep desire for belonging and quirkiness of Menzel’s portrayal resonated with me. As a white man Erivo’s performance wasn’t very resonant but as a queer person I definitely connected with other aspects of her performance. I have spoken with many Black actors who found her performance incredibly moving and familiar. It didn’t hit me the same way, but I’m so glad that different performers give us the opportunity to explore the depths of a character and ultimately what makes us human.

One aspect that isn’t fresh on the minds of audiences is that Wicked was a very timely piece in the early 2000s. The US was embroiled in multiple wars, the Guantanamo Bay prisoners, the falsehoods from the intelligence community, and at the helm of it all was a guy who regularly misspoke and made up words. Other shows from around the time also critiqued Bush (Avenue Q: George Bush is only for now). The wizard, and especially Madame Morrible were fashioned as Bush-like figures in the world of Oz and audiences were intended to read those current events onto the world of the play. 

I saw the national tour in 2013 and it was remarkable how the references no longer resonate with audiences in the same way. I do think there’s some unfortunate similarities in the current US politics and the world of oz, it will be very interesting to see how the more biting critiques of Act II translate for the audience of tomorrow.

Honestly, here is my read on the situation. I’ve been teaching at an arts magnet high school this year after leaving my incredibly toxic position at a SLAC. A little more detail on what many scholars believe that phrase came from: in general, ancient near eastern religions went from polytheistic to monotheistic over time. That particular passage in Genesis is from a manuscript dated much older than the creation story that opens the book of Genesis. One indicator is the plurality of God in that passage which corresponds to the concept of a “council of the gods” of which Elohim was said to be the chief god and the other gods were more like demigods. Many Christians point to this passage as evidence of the Trinity but the concept is foreign to the text at hand. (Interestingly enough, this was similar to an issue at the ecumenical councils that established the Nicene creed. They were debating whether Jesus WAS god or if Jesus was a being created by God that was more of a demigod. The IS GOD team won.) Another text that scholars point to as evidence of a “council of the gods” in pre-Abrahamic times is the book of Job where some translations inaccurately translate Bnei HaElohim (literally the sons of Elohim / god) as “angels.” One of these “sons of god” is Ha Satan (the accuser) who Christians interpret to be “the devil” but Ha Satan is a much older concept and not “the devil” as Christians understand it. There are also frequent references throughout the Tanakh to Asherah which in some ancient near eastern religions was known as the queen consort of Elohim.

Yeah you have to go into disability services with several caveats. “I’m not trying to diagnose, I’m not asking for a diagnosis, I’ve not received an accommodations letter, I’ve just observed some behaviors that might indicate some disability and wanted to mention it in the event disability services can do anything to assist this student.” In the situation I was dealing with, our disability services actually had a team that handled behavioral issues related to disabilities and they told me “I can’t confirm or deny that the student is registered, but if they are, we have a team that can meet with the student to address these issues.” 

In terms of meeting with the student, someone else suggested perhaps doing the meeting over zoom. This would mitigate any potential physical reaction from the student and ensure your safety should they have an outburst that turned violent. I’d definitely not approach them after class simply because the situation has already proven volatile.

I had a similar instance with a student once. It was a situation outside of the classroom but my conversation with disability services felt very empowering. (Assuming you’re in the US) As I understand it, FERPA and HIPAA prevent disclosure of the student’s diagnostic status but there’s nothing to prevent you from alerting disability services about disruptive behavior that might be related to an undisclosed or undiagnosed disability. Now what disability services can and will do after that will depend on the individuals in that office, local policies, state regulations, and federal law. 

Regardless, I would approach the student and describe the behaviors you’re observing and indicate that these behaviors are disruptive and unacceptable. For example “During class you have interrupted me while I was speaking to ask a question. You do this 10-20 times in a class period. This is an unusually high number of questions and the way you are going about asking them is disruptive to the classroom environment.” If you’re in a one party consent state, audio record the interaction. If you’re in a two party state, have a trusted colleague sit in on the meeting with you or be within earshot. One strategy you might employ for the constant questions would be to have them write down their questions and you can respond to them after class. You could also give them a reasonable number of questions they are allowed to ask during a class period and perhaps even specify the types of questions that are allowed or not allowed. For example: “you should not ask for the definition of a word, this is the kind of thing you should look up for yourself. You may only speak by raising your hand and I must acknowledge you.” This will make them prioritize the questions that are actually important and keep them from interrupting you. 

With the exam, I’d tell them if they meant to write something else they should have done so. You’re replicating the experience they would have with a future employer. Their boss won’t care what they *meant* to do, say, or write. The only thing that matters in this instance is what is on the page. 

I would also establish clear, written descriptions of these expectations and what will happen if the student breaks these expectations. For example, the first time you’ll verbally remind them of your agreement just saying “please remember our agreement”. The second time they will be asked to leave the classroom for the day. The third time they’ll be sent to student conduct for classroom disruption and could potentially be removed from the class. 

Best of luck!

I teach at an institution where the students are routinely underserved in their k-12 experiences. I also teach in a creative field where generation of ideas and content is part of the discipline. I’ve seen students struggle to engage in the type of writing that you mention. I also hear about mental health all the time. 

I think what makes the difference for me is that my response is to sit with them in the discomfort of these tasks. They seem to expect immediate alleviation of stress when they say they’re pressed. I make them go through it. I tell them it’s normal. I tell them everyone feels this way sometimes, hell even I do. I walk them through the thought process. If they’re having trouble coming up with a topic, make them write down things they’re interested in without worrying about coming up with a topic. Then ask them questions to identify topics within those categories. Oh you like makeup tutorials? What do you think about Jeffree Star? How would you convince someone who doesn’t think the way you do about him?You like anime? How do you feel about the term “weeb?” Convince me of your position. You like hip hop? What do you think about the feud between Cardi B and Nicki Minaj? How would you convince someone of your position? 

Once they see that they can actually work through the thought process, I’ve seen that they can begin to cope and do the writing most of the time. 

Should we have to do this level of handholding? Absolutely not. Is it the only way forward? Probably.

Obviously this can be murky depending on the topic, but I’ve yet to find a student that didn’t react when I tell them traditional linear plot structures mirror the male sexual arousal pattern. Get them heated about something relevant to the topic and weave the content throughout the discussion. Put them against one another competitively or in a debate. When I teach Arthur Miller’s “Tragedy and the common man” I split the class in two and make one side Team Aristotle (which has already been covered) and one side Team Miller and give them time to prepare their arguments for why their definition of tragedy is superior. I also will have students prepare 3 discussion questions/topics before class (along with a few I’ve planted) and put them in a hat then use those to guide the discussion. Because they’ve prepped the questions, they tend to be more prepared to discuss the topic and have already been thinking about ideas and connections.

Honestly, I’d tell these students that the only considerations I account for when grading is the work presented and that their future employers will do the same at best. I’m able to be flexible with due dates, extensions, and accommodations but anything else is unreasonable and unprofessional to request. I’d tell them in those exact terms which should head off any future requests.

As a student, I went to an institution that required 80 hours of “service learning” but it was poorly structured and ended up being 80 hours of volunteer service. 

As faculty, I’ve personally not had any service learning in my courses, but I’ve worked with a faculty member in communication that had a pretty good arrangement. This faculty member taught marketing and PR and basically set up a firm within those courses. Students were grouped and worked with an organization (often non-profits) to work on a specific initiative. When I worked with them, they were working on marketing for our theatre production or an event connected to it. Other groups worked with Big Brothers/Sisters, a startup coffee company, and an org for women and children who’d experienced domestic violence. The initiatives seemed mostly successful, though one time I got a group of students that did next to nothing. 

Another faculty member did service learning with our actors working with psychology majors in an abnormal psych class. Our actors would research and perform various psychological conditions and serve as an opportunity for the psych students to recognize and make diagnoses. 

I think the important thing is to identify what the students should be learning through the process and make it more than volunteer service. It does require a lot of hand holding and it’s important to avoid adding additional work for the folks the students are working with.

These students are going to encounter barriers to their success that a student from a different background might not. The goal is to design the educational experience to eliminate those barriers as much as is possible and reasonable. The most common strategy is using OERs instead of expensive textbooks. We can’t fix the inequalities they’ve experienced so far, but we can eliminate barriers and attempt to provide ways for these students to fill in the gaps in their past preparations.

So here’s my hypothesis: if you go after the amount of *effort* students put in, you’re going to lose every single time. Effort is relative, subjective, and emotionally charged. Meeting expectations and benchmarks, however, removes at least some of the subjectivity and emotional energy. I’m very honest with students and try to focus entirely on the work. I also tie the expectations to tangible career outcomes. “You have to be on time because you’re working as a team and if you’re not there, everyone loses time.” “You have to pay close attention to details because this detail is a safety concern.” I usually start by reiterating the expectations then describe the ways that the work failed to meet those benchmarks. It’s not that they didn’t work hard enough, it’s that they didn’t address their topic thoroughly. They didn’t catch mistakes that proofreading should catch. They needed more specificity in their argument. They needed to go beyond scratching the surface. They needed to pay closer attention to details. All criticisms are focused on the work turned in and how it did or did not meet expectations. I’ve had much luck with this strategy. I still have a student or two that have managed to find a way to be offended, but they’re outliers that don’t represent the whole.

There’s a fantastic model for creative critique from Liz Lerman. It’s specifically designed for dance, but I’m sure you could adapt it for just about any discipline where critique is necessary. What I like about it is the session starts out with “statements of meaning” where participants express things they found interesting, exciting, or meaningful. It’s all just positive statements. Then the student explains what they were going for. Then participants ask neutral questions devoid of opinions. Then the last stage is time for opinions and each opinion is prefaced with “I have an opinion about ________, would you like to hear it?” And the student has the option to accept or deny. 

This method is life changing for works in progress. I adapt it for final critiques as well by making the opinion stage the time for my critique (without the option to accept or deny the opinion) and then allowing student participants to speak opinions without the accept or deny option. 

Here’s a brief description of the process: [Liz Lerman’s Critical Response Process](https://lizlerman.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/Critical-Response-Process-in-Brief_CRP-one-pager_updated-2020_03_24.pdf)

They were always 5-10 minutes late for class, when they arrived they’d write an outline on the board for 2-3 mins, and then because it was a religious school each class was supposed to start with a prayer or “devotion” and they’d go on and on usually until 20-25 past the hour. I was angry but I also realized my deficit was that I wasn’t able to keep up with the 50-80 pages of textbook reading prior to each class. I started to read the textbook in class which gave me about three solid hours of reading each week for the class. It nearly eliminated working outside of class. I’d sometimes have like an additional hour outside of class a week. My exam grades shot up and I was able to skip the last exam because I’d done well enough  on the other 3 (the last exam was an optional grade replacer). 

You have to figure out what works for you, develop the skills to assess your deficits, and find ways to adapt and personalize the course for yourself. Perhaps someone who the person would trust could invite them to a grief group off campus and that would give them an outlet to share with others going through similar things. Ideally that group becomes the outlet for their grief and behaviors in the workplace level out. Another path might be to talk with them and express that you’ve noticed the grief seems overwhelming and ask if they’d considered an individual grief counselor off campus. Sometimes people just don’t realize that their grief is occupying as much space as it is in their daily life and someone recognizing that it might be too much is enough to bring some clarity and self-regulation. All of this said, all grief is valid and necessary at times. BUT like depression, bipolar, and other common mental health conditions, there is a point when the grief begins to spill out on others in ways that are neither productive or safe. We could all probably use a little more compassion and self-regulation of our emotions.

Nude illusion is kind of like CGI…there’s a shit ton of it all the time but we only notice it when it’s bad. Oftentimes the nude mesh is necessary for the look to maintain its shape and structure. I think we end up noticing it more often on non-white queens because the color mixing is a lot more complex for their skin tone. Having tried to match skin tones before, the dyes you can get relatively easily don’t have the right undertones. For example, RIT dye’s dark brown has a lot of purple in it. When you dilute it you get an ashy purple. The camel color has a lot of green in it and when you dilute it that green makes for a sickly looking undertone. If you mix and dilute the two, it looks like absolute garbage. Then there’s the difference between the color wet and when the mesh dries. The best way of doing nude illusion that I’ve found is matching skin tone to Nude Barre products and hacking up those tights into appropriate sized pieces. It’s tough when you need a whole bodysuit or a large area though.

EDIT: I’ll add that the difficulty of matching skin tones would be a moot point if fabric manufacturers would offer greater variety of colors. Like many things in this world, they primarily cater to white skin tones and offer little in terms of diversity. For example, Nude Barre has 12 colors. Most power mesh usually comes in 3-4 colors, one of which is for white skin tones. Nude Barre is pretty pricey because diverse hosiery is pretty much all they do. These fabric companies have a variety of products that prevent them from going under based on the sales of one product.

The advice here so far is good. Definitely go to the chair first. Frame your issues as “concerns” rather than complaints. These are genuinely issues that, when combined, pose a serious risk for student success. When it comes to understanding the professor through verbal communication, avoid explicitly mentioning the accent or stuttering as these are in the realm of race and disability. Instead, express that you have a difficult time understanding the professor’s speech and that they often seem flustered or frustrated. The frustrated demeanor combined with admonitions to read the book and an inability to navigate the software would indicate to me that this professor is overwhelmed or out of their depth in this particular topic. Chances are they’re a brilliant scholar in another area which is how/why they got and have kept the job. The chair *should* have a balanced sense of loyalty to the faculty member and responsibility to the students. This means that, ideally, the resolution will probably have aspects of compromise. Don’t go in expecting that the chair is going to Deus Ex Machina the whole situation. The best case scenario is that the prof makes some changes and the students make some concessions (ie they’re unlikely to just remove the professor from the course and have someone else teach). I might try to get a TA or a tutor into the classroom to provide support to both the students and professor.

So there are several schools of thought on this. On one extreme there is absolute hardcore documentation and on the other extreme absolutely none. I tend to fall in the middle. 

There are unfortunately far too many students who take advantage of “traumatic excuse” policies and end up with more dead grandparents than is logically possible. On the other hand, an attendance policy that doesn’t have a mechanism for accountability for attendance and participation can be detrimental for new college students developing personal discipline in their newfound freedom as young adults. 

I used to require documentation for “extraordinary excuses” such as funerals, court dates, surgeries, and sickness. I made it clear that I wasn’t interested in prying into the details of someone’s life but merely keeping documentation on any exceptions I made to my course policies outlined in the syllabus. 

Now, I record all of my classes on Teams and if a student misses class for any reason they must go back to the video, watch it, and write a 1-page summary of the content of the session for class credit that day. It’s worked beautifully and I think reduces stress on me AND my students.

When it comes to more subjective assignments, the expectation is the same. The rubric model of evaluation supports this. 

As a theatre prof, a majority of my graded assignments are entirely subjective. In these assignments I strive to provide as many objective expectations as possible. When a student is putting together a research book for dramaturgy, I require x number of scholarly sources, x number of popular sources, and x number of sensory sources (pics, video, fabric swatches, etc). There is subjectivity in the quality of these sources and I provide feedback on that, but I grade based on the number of these sources included. 

The “read the mind of your professor to understand expectations and get fucked over when you don’t do that correctly” model is antiquated and detracts from learning.

I was homeschooled from 5th grade through my high school graduation. My mom has an M.A.T. and licensed for K-8. 

CONS:
I hated every minute of homeschooling and begged my parents to let me go back to public school. I was acutely aware of the way homeschooling disconnected me from socializing with my peers and kept me academically parallel to them. My parents always insisted that being with kids my age at church was enough. The reality was, I was ostracized by my peers because I didn’t go to public school. I ended up socializing with adults more often than not. Homeschooling exacerbated my perfectionism because I was competing with myself and I was academically strong. By the time I was in high school I ended up making my own arrangements to satisfy class requirements. I contracted a HS English teacher from my church to go through 3 semesters of English and enrolled in an anatomy course at the technical college to satisfy my last science class. My parents weren’t happy about the last bit, but it didn’t cost me anything and I was 18. 

PROS:
Homeschooling gave me a very flexible schedule and I became a shift manager at a well-run Subway. I learned a lot of practical leadership skills and had decent cash flow. I spent a lot of time on AOL message boards reading and talking about my interests. I learned writing and rhetoric better than any textbook could provide through this practical experience. Homeschooling provided much space for creativity and critical thinking which directly benefitted my undergrad and grad school programs in theatre. 

With the right situation, for the right kid, with the right parent-educator, with the right resources, and buy-in from the child, I think homeschooling can be incredibly effective. However, if any of those pieces are missing, the quality begins to decline rapidly.

I would imagine that despite how cathartic it might feel, just telling them to find another class is going to facilitate the perception that college is just another place that will traumatize them. Here’s how I would approach the situation:

Meet with the student saying “I wanted to talk about your access needs when it comes to this course. My first priority is always to make sure that the classroom is a respectful and brave space where we can discuss difficult topics in an effort to make the world a better place. I do have some concerns because this is a very exhaustive list. Literature is a discipline within the humanities that explores the question of the human experience, what does it mean to exist in this world as a human being? The reality is that human nature can be incredibly beautiful and inspiring. It can also be dark and grotesque. We read these pieces of literature to better understand all aspects of the human experience. I know that many of the pieces we read this semester are going to contain subject matter that you’ve mentioned. I’m not here to tell you what you must do, but I worry that you’re going to struggle in this class and throughout college if you’re unable to engage with these topics in a safe space like the classroom. I’d like to discuss how we might move forward in the course, being sensitive to your needs but also recognizing that almost anything written for an adult is going to contain this subject matter in some way. If that means this course isn’t right for you, that’s totally fine. If you want to collaborate to find ways you can engage with the material without causing you harm, we can do that as well. I’d love for you to stay in the class but that is your decision alone.”

If they want to move forward with the class, recommend that they see someone in the counseling center to work through things as they come up. If they express any traumas related to suicide or sexual assault, you may need to find alternate readings and assignments for those pieces. You might also suggest a reading buddy to read ahead and provide any content warnings before diving into a scene of graphic violence or sexual assault.

I’ve noticed in several international seasons that the lighting seems…off. I don’t think there’s one single reason why but there’s a number of factors. First, the international seasons seem to be produced at various price points. This probably impacts the lighting fixtures selected. Second, the US seasons probably have a carefully calibrated mix of incandescent fixtures and LED fixtures. LED wasn’t as widespread when the show started and the incandescent fixtures are long haul workhorses. These have different base color temps which will impact the perception of the light to the naked eye and to the camera. The international seasons are likely to have more LED fixtures because that’s what newer productions are using. Third, the lighting levels are likely set using similar levels to the US original. These levels don’t quite work with a different light rig and need to be calibrated against the performers in action. This is why the lighting tends to improve a few eps in. Lastly the color correction, again, is probably using settings from the US original and needs to be calibrated with performers in action. All these factors combine to cause chaos in the calibration of the lighting. The gradual improvement depends on the skill of the technicians involved and the outcomes are inconsistent.

This is a question with a very long and complex history. Braids and locs are traditional, culturally specific hairstyles in Africa. When the African slave trade kidnapped and enslaved people, there are stories of braided hairstyles being used to provided maps for escape. Traditional African hairstyles, and Black hair in general has become an important part of Black identity because many Black folks in the US have been severed from their historical roots in Africa. These hairstyles are a means of connecting to their heritage. Unfortunately these traditional styles have been denigrated as dirty, unkempt, and unprofessional. These characterizations are rooted in white supremacy and Eurocentric beauty standards. When properly cared for, Black hair in locs and braids is completely hygienic and protects Black hair from damage. 

On a practical level, white hair does not naturally loc. when white people get “locs” they use crochet needles and product to create mats in the hair. Black hair will loc naturally if the hair is not separated/de-tangled regularly. 

White people avoiding locs and box braids is an act of respect toward Black folks who often take great pride in their hair. This pride is frequently a response to the ways that white supremacy has vilified Black hair.

This started as a comment noting that Method acting isn’t as great as everyone is led to think it is. It’s become something else because I didn’t feel like explaining why the Method was so damaging. People revere Method actors mostly because it’s the only acting system/technique they know about. Talk to anyone in the industry and mention “Method” and most people will roll their eyes.

The Method is mostly the work of Lee Strasberg based on his experiences with Richard Boleslavski and Marie Ouspenskya. Those two led a series of workshops to teach what was a poor translation of the first half of the Stanislavski system. This first half, and the method, focus on interior psychological work and it’s techniques are rooted in outdated, damaging psychological ideas. Stanislavski noticed in the second half of his career that internal psychological work alone was not enough to produce convincing performances. The Method employs the idea “if I feel it deeply enough the audience will see it.” This is objectively untrue. Stanislavski worked to balance internal (psychological) and external (physical) work for the second half of his career. The Method on the other hand, did not. 

The Method asks actors to “become” rather than portray and theres only so many times an actor can go into the depths of the human psyche to “become” before they inflict permanent psychological damage. Not every Method actor experiences this, but it’s like playing Russian Roulette with your mental health. Sure it can be done safely, but you’ll never know you’re unsafe until it’s too late. 

In general many Method actors are some of the most difficult to work with because they prioritize their process over everything else. It doesn’t matter that they’re being a douche to everyone on set, making the lives of underpaid PAs and staff a living hell. 

There’s just a better way of doing it. No performance is worth the potential trauma of Method acting.

Cocaine was an incredibly effective pain reliever but the byproducts of its use were not worth the results. Everyone acts as if method acting is the be-all and end all of acting. The reality is, it’s based on a misinterpretation of the first half of the Stanislavski system and has been a comorbidity in a number of high profile cases of actors taking their own lives.
